b: Accessibility Accessibility statement Last updated October 2026 Our aim We want everyone to be able to use thecareleaders.com, including people who use a screen reader, a keyboard, magnification or voice control. We build the site to the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 at level AA. What we’ve done Text and buttons meet the contrast levels in WCAG 2.2 AA. Every page works with a keyboard and shows where you are with a visible focus outline. Buttons and links are large enough to tap. Text can be enlarged to 200% without losing content, and the layout works on phones. Images that carry meaning have text descriptions, and videos only load when you choose to play them. What we know still needs work Some brochures and reports you can download are PDFs designed for print, and may not work well with a screen reader. Some case studies show photos of documents and slides, and the words in those images aren’t always repeated on the page. If you need any of this in another format, ask us and we’ll send it. Tell us about a problem If something on the site doesn’t work for you, or you need information in a different format, email hello@thecareleaders.com . We’ll reply within 5 working days.

That meant giving staff something to do instead: a way to stay calm and present when a young person’s behaviour escalates, and to repair the relationship afterwards. What we did Step 1 Online Two modules on The Care Leaders Online: NVR principles, the Seven Pillars and preparation for the workshops Step 2 Workshop 1 De-escalation and reconciliation gestures, run morning and afternoon so homes kept safe staffing Step 3 Workshop 2 Acts of resistance and sit-ins Reach 120 staff, 11 homes From launch in September 2025 to the close of the programme We designed the programme around the realities of residential care. Every member of staff completed two online modules on The Care Leaders Online, covering NVR principles, the Seven Pillars and preparation for the face-to-face sessions. They then attended two half-day workshops on de-escalation, reconciliation gestures, acts of resistance and sit-ins. We ran each workshop in the morning and again in the afternoon, so homes could keep safe staffing levels. b: Luke Speaks Keynotes and conference workshops with Luke Rodgers BEM I went into care at 10. At 15 I was living in a B&B, and at 18 I was in a caravan. I gave my first keynote at 19, standing in front of a room of professionals and telling them what care had felt like from the inside. I’ve been doing it ever since, because it’s still one of the fastest ways I know to change how people see children in care. That’s why I set up The Care Leaders: to go from care leaver to care leader, and to help others make the same move. Since then I’ve led the national engagement on England’s new fostering standards, been a Knowledge Equity Fellow at Saïd Business School, Oxford, and been awarded the British Empire Medal. Every talk brings together stories of care from my lived experience, the theory behind it and tools your audience can use the next day. Length 6 hours face to face, or 2 hours online Group Up to 60 face to face, 200 online For Primary, secondary and special schools Included Workbook, 12 months online, certificate Add to shortlist On your shortlist Ask about this course View your shortlist The problem it solves The DfE’s statutory guidance for designated teachers asks them to make sure school staff have high expectations. b: Supporting Boys in Care: training for carers, schools and youth justice Boys in care need to be seen too. Training that helps your team stay alongside boys in care when they push adults away. You leave with a team action plan with named actions and a review date. Length 6 hours face to face, or 2 hours online Group Up to 60 face to face, 200 online For Carers, children’s homes, schools and youth justice Included Workbook, 12 months online, certificate Add to shortlist On your shortlist Ask about this course View your shortlist The problem it solves The DfE’s figures for 2025 show boys make up 56% of children in care in England. Many have learned that anger is safer to show than fear or sadness. Adults often meet that anger with a sanction, a police call or a move. The 2018 national protocol on reducing unnecessary criminalisation of looked-after children and care leavers is clear. Carers should deal with low-level incidents at home, as a reasonable parent would. Staff need the skills and backing.
